Ransomware Attack Disrupts Cayman Islands Agriculture Firms, Workers Face Uncertainty

GEORGE TOWN, Cayman Islands, June 10 – Multiple agriculture firms across the Cayman Islands are struggling to operate after a ransomware attack crippled key IT systems on Monday, halting crop management, payroll processing, and supply tracking at several sites, industry officials said.

The Cayman Agricultural Producers Association (CAPA) confirmed that at least four major firms, including Greenway Farms Ltd and Island Harvest Co, have been affected by the ongoing cyber incident. The attack, detected early Monday morning, has locked employees out of digital management platforms used for crop scheduling, irrigation control, and inventory records. 

“Digital systems are at the heart of almost every aspect of our operations now, from tracking shipments to monitoring greenhouse conditions,” said CAPA President Marsha Ebanks in a statement. “With access cut off, we are relying on manual processes where possible, but it is causing major delays and confusion on the ground.”

Greenway Farms Ltd, which operates three sites on Grand Cayman, reported that hundreds of workers were sent home Monday as managers scrambled to assess the extent of the breach. Island Harvest Co said it had suspended harvesting at two of its largest fields due to an inability to access planting and yield data.

A worker at one affected site, who asked not to be named due to company policy, described uncertainty among staff. “We don’t know when things will be back to normal or if we’ll be paid on time this week. The office can’t access payroll or scheduling at all,” the employee said.

The Ministry of Agriculture confirmed it is working with local law enforcement and cybersecurity consultants to investigate the incident. “At this stage, we do not have evidence of data theft, but the attack has rendered several firms’ core systems inoperable,” said a spokesperson.

Industry analysts say the Cayman Islands’ agriculture sector, which produces a range of crops including tomatoes, sweet potatoes, peppers, and bananas, has rapidly digitized in recent years to boost yields and improve efficiency. This shift, experts warn, has made the industry more vulnerable to cyber threats.

“Ransomware attackers are increasingly targeting sectors like agriculture, where downtime can lead to immediate and significant losses,” said Dr. Carlene Russell, a regional cybersecurity researcher. “Recovery may take days or weeks, depending on the robustness of firms’ backups and response plans.”

As of late Monday, no group had claimed responsibility, and CAPA said negotiations with the attackers had not begun. Firms are urging workers to remain home until further notice, with updates expected as the situation develops.
